name: Digital credential infrastructure
definition: Digital credential infrastructure connects institution-governed award approval, issuance, verification and record maintenance with supported interfaces and related records.
problem: When award rules, issuance permissions and verification procedures are disconnected, teams can issue inconsistent records or leave correction responsibilities unclear.
architecture: Award approval, issuance, proof and status checks, and record maintenance form a connected credential lifecycle. Registrars retain authority over award data, academic teams approve assessed meaning, and IT supports access and compatible interfaces.
how: CertifyMe connects institution-approved achievement information with supported credential formats, recipient delivery and verification. Corrections, dates, evidence access and applicable status remain part of the record lifecycle.
standards: Open Badges 3.0 describes achievement credentials; W3C Verifiable Credentials describes issuer, holder and verifier roles. Supported formats and proof mechanisms enable exchange with compatible receiving systems.
implementation: A governed programme brings approval, issuance, recipient access, verification and record maintenance together. API and integration scope, security controls and deployment terms are aligned with the institution's systems.
use_case: Universities can govern academic and co-curricular awards; certification bodies can govern professional achievements; enterprise and training teams can manage assessed programme recognition. The award criteria determine what is actually supported.
example: A department awards an assessed project-completion credential after approval, keeps sensitive feedback in an authorized system and defines who handles a correction.
limitation: An issuance platform does not independently prove a learner's competence, issuer accreditation or real-world identity. Keys, status resources and receiving-system support can remain dependencies.

faq.question: Is infrastructure just a certificate designer?
faq.answer: No. Presentation is one component; governance, verification, lifecycle responsibilities and supported record interfaces are separate requirements.

faq.question: Does every programme need every connected feature?
faq.answer: Different programmes use different combinations of credential formats, skills, records and interfaces. The institution's awards and receiving systems determine the relevant capabilities.

name: Open Badges 3.0
definition: Open Badges 3.0 describes digital achievement credentials that identify an issuer, achievement and related criteria/evidence within a verifiable-credential context.
problem: A badge image can be easy to share while leaving its achievement, assessment and verification requirements unclear. Institutions need the record and governance behind the presentation.
architecture: An Open Badges record connects issuer, recipient, achievement, criteria, evidence and supported proof. Receiving systems interpret that structured information according to their own policies.
how: CertifyMe's certified OB3 Issuer role supports the issuance of structured achievements that authorized holders can present to compatible verifiers for proof and status checks.
standards: Open Badges 3.0 applies the 1EdTech specification within a verifiable-credential context. CertifyMe's Open Badges 3.0 Issuer certification is listed in the public 1EdTech registry.
implementation: Institution-approved achievements can be represented with structured criteria and evidence, giving recipients a shareable record that receiving systems can interpret when their formats and proof mechanisms are compatible.
use_case: A faculty may recognize an assessed laboratory milestone; a professional body may recognize development activity. Distinguish attendance, completion and demonstrated competence in the criteria.
example: An assessed research-proposal milestone connects the achievement with its criteria and evidence, while the institution controls access to reviewer feedback.
limitation: OB3 conformance does not establish assessment quality, independent recipient identity or universal portability. Verification may retain issuer-key and status-resource dependencies.

faq.question: Does OB3 issuer certification certify every receiving platform?
faq.answer: No. Issuer certification covers the listed issuer product and role. Receiving platforms have their own supported formats and proof mechanisms.

faq.question: Does a badge necessarily prove a skill?
faq.answer: Only the achievement and assessment stated by the issuer are supported; a skill relationship requires review.

name: W3C Verifiable Credentials
definition: The W3C Verifiable Credentials data model describes structured issuer claims and issuer, holder and verifier roles; an appropriate securing mechanism supports proof checks.
problem: A receiving organization needs to separate the claim, its proof and the issuer's authority rather than accepting a visually convincing document.
architecture: The credential data model, securing mechanism, issuer resources and receiving policy serve distinct roles. Together they give a receiving organisation the information needed to interpret an issued claim.
how: A verifier checks a supported proof and relevant dates/status resources, then evaluates whether the issuer and achievement meet its policy. Successful proof checking is not the whole acceptance decision.
standards: The W3C data model describes issuer claims; Open Badges supplies achievement context and a CLR connects related records with provenance. Proof mechanisms depend on the implemented profile.
implementation: A verifiable-credential workflow connects a supported proof with issuer information, dates and applicable status. Continued access to issuer keys, evidence and compatible receiving systems supports long-term interpretation.
use_case: Universities and professional bodies can present supported achievements to a verifier; the verifier still assesses issuer authority and purpose-specific requirements.
example: A learner presents a course-completion record. The receiving organization checks its proof, reviews the course against its requirements and confirms the recipient's identity.
limitation: A valid proof may accompany an unsuitable or unsupported claim. Standards do not guarantee universal receiver compatibility, issuer-independent availability or independent real-world identity verification.

faq.question: Is verifiable the same as independently true?
faq.answer: No. Proof checking supports integrity and signing authority, while issuer, assessment and policy questions remain.

faq.question: Are issuer resources always unnecessary?
faq.answer: No. Keys and applicable status resources can remain dependencies; continuity must be assessed.

name: Skills taxonomy mapping
definition: Skills taxonomy mapping relates institution-defined outcomes and assessed achievement evidence to reviewed capability concepts in local or reference vocabularies.
problem: Course titles, credential labels and occupational skill terms can sound similar without describing the same assessed capability. Institutions need accountable review of the relationship.
architecture: Programme → learning outcome → achievement evidence → credential → reviewed skill → learner record → occupation → separately sourced workforce demand. Academic meaning and market signals retain their distinct sources.
how: Institution-reviewed relationships connect assessed outcomes to ESCO, O*NET or local concepts, preserving the rationale and provenance behind each mapping.
standards: ESCO, O*NET and custom competency frameworks provide reference vocabularies; they are not automatic proof of competence or a verified native integration. Credential and record formats preserve the issued claim's context.
implementation: Academic owners govern outcome-to-skill relationships as programmes and reference vocabularies change. The issued achievement retains the assessed meaning; the skill relationship adds interpretable context.
use_case: Academic leadership can examine curriculum relevance; career services can help learners explain assessed capabilities; a certification body can describe qualification evidence consistently.
example: A rubric-assessed data-cleaning project connects a learning achievement with a specific capability and its academic review rationale.
limitation: A taxonomy link is a conceptual relationship, not an independent competency or employment examination. Market data, identity checking and assessment are separate evidence questions.

faq.question: Can a taxonomy match prove competence?
faq.answer: No. Assessment evidence and institutional review determine what was demonstrated.

faq.question: Must external vocabulary replace our academic language?
faq.answer: No. Retain institutional meaning and document reviewed relationships to external concepts.

name: Comprehensive Learner Record
definition: A Comprehensive Learner Record connects achievements and related evidence with provenance in an institution-governed learner record.
problem: A transcript, individual badge and co-curricular achievement can describe different parts of a learner's experience. Connecting them should not erase who issued or assessed each item.
architecture: A connected learner record preserves the issuer, criteria and evidence behind each achievement. The SIS and transcript retain their separately governed authoritative roles.
how: CertifyMe connects achievements and reviewed skills relationships in a learner-facing record with issuer provenance, supported access, correction and export workflows.
standards: CLR is a 1EdTech learner-record standard related to Open Badges and W3C credential concepts. CertifyMe's CLR 2.0 Issuer and Displayer roles are listed in the 1EdTech registry.
implementation: Registrars, academic teams and IT bring their established record and access responsibilities to a connected learner journey. Learners can present achievements without replacing the institution's official academic record.
use_case: A university may connect academic, assessed project and co-curricular achievements. Career services may help a learner present relevant evidence while preserving issuer boundaries.
example: A learner record brings together a course achievement and an assessed project, preserving each award's criteria, evidence and source.
limitation: A CLR does not automatically replace a transcript, SIS or every receiving organization's requirements. Aggregating records is not independent verification of all underlying claims.

faq.question: Is a CLR a transcript replacement?
faq.answer: Not automatically. Institutions define authoritative roles; the CLR can complement academic and operational records.

faq.question: Does a connected record independently prove every skill?
faq.answer: No. Each achievement and reviewed relationship retains its original assessment and evidence boundary.

name: Workforce intelligence
definition: Institutional workforce intelligence relates reviewed skills and achievements to occupations and separately sourced employer-demand information.
problem: Curriculum evidence and market vocabulary may not align directly. Institutions need to examine relevance without treating a job posting or a skill-term match as proof of attainment.
architecture: Assessed achievement evidence, reviewed skill relationships, occupations and employer-demand sources remain distinct layers with their own provenance.
how: CertifyMe relates reviewed credential-associated skills to occupational context and separately sourced job information, helping academic and career-service teams explore relevant opportunities.
standards: Reference vocabularies such as ESCO and O*NET can support reviewed occupation relationships. They do not certify employer demand, learner competence or a native connector.
implementation: Academic and career-service teams can relate programme skills to occupational requirements and employer-demand context. Available data fields, geography and salary information depend on the sources used for each report.
use_case: Programme leaders can investigate curriculum relevance; career services can support opportunity research; learners can explain achievements and investigate gaps without an employment guarantee.
example: Compare project-related capabilities with occupational descriptions and recent employer requirements to guide curriculum planning and career conversations.
limitation: CertifyMe's job-farming engine covers 20 million live jobs from 50,000 companies worldwide, refreshed every two weeks. Geography and available report fields depend on the source data. Occupational context supports opportunity research; hiring remains an employer decision.

faq.question: Does workforce information prove job readiness?
faq.answer: No. Assessment, reviewed mapping, current opportunity suitability and hiring decisions are separate questions.

faq.question: Is the job dataset refreshed in real time?
faq.answer: The dataset is refreshed every two weeks, keeping job and company context updated on that cadence.
